analysis:
The PR changes the runner label of four Ubuntu-only jobs in .github/workflows/release-provider.yml from blacksmith-4vcpu-ubuntu-2404 to GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04. The jobs are resolve-env (head line 135), qualify-sdk (304), stage-release (~1211) and publish-release (~1320). It also adds timeout-minutes: 90 to build-and-release (head 343). The macOS signing, build and notarization jobs stay on blacksmith-12vcpu-macos-27.

Security-relevant observations from the visible units:
- resolve-env still checks out master and runs verify-source before any credential-consuming job, so the trust gate is unchanged (base lines 150-163).
- stage-release and publish-release handle R2 and release-key secrets, which now run on GitHub-hosted ephemeral runners instead of Blacksmith runners. The visible excerpt shows no change to the secret scoping, the env-gated PROD_/STAGING_ secret expressions, or the permissions blocks. GitHub-hosted runners are ephemeral and isolated per job, so this does not obviously weaken A-005, A-011 or A-017 custody. The Blacksmith-to-GitHub-hosted trust-domain change is a deployment choice; no threat-model claim about it is visible. The stage-release and publish-release bodies are not in the supplied units, so I could not re-verify them.
- The signing-keychain handling (base lines 643-718) is unchanged. Adding a 90-minute timeout to build-and-release bounds the job's availability exposure and keeps the signing key from lingering on a hung runner; the keychain cleanup is not conditioned on an always() step in the visible lines, which is pre-existing.
- The qualify-sdk job still audits shard counts; its runner change does not alter the checks.
- No action pins changed in the visible changes.

Remaining questions for integration: confirm that the stage-release and publish-release step bodies, which are only partially excerpted, do not depend on Blacksmith-specific tooling or network egress allowlists. Also confirm that the pinned GitHub CLI or other tool assumptions hold on ubuntu-24.04. These are operational, not security regressions. I found no concrete security regression.
